source.title: Asymptotic Unbiased Sample Sampling to Speed Up Sharpness-Aware Minimization
source.authors: Jia-Xin Deng; Jun-Biao Pang; Bao-Chang Zhang; Guo-Dong Guo

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendix text provided.
record.tranche_reason: Applies a new sample-selection training method to image classification, pose estimation, and quantization, and reports held-out performance; it does not test the specific versions listed.
record.gate_note: The study reports held-out accuracy for SAM, AUSAM, SGD, and comparison methods. Its own claimed sample-selection results are included; comparison methods reported from prior work are not treated as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study uses the flatness–generalization rationale to develop and evaluate a faster SAM method. Its results compare task accuracy and training speed, without testing any of V1–V8. In particular, optimizing unscaled SAM sharpness does not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness ranking of generalization gaps. Changing sample selection and effective batch size together does not isolate V5's large-batch effect.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors' conclusion: selecting samples with larger estimated gradient norms accelerates SAM while approximately preserving performance across classification, pose estimation and quantization. Their broad comparable-performance and approximately 70% speedup claims require qualification by architecture and sampling rate: for example, ResNet-50 on Tiny-ImageNet falls from 67.69 to 66.60, and ResNet-18 CIFAR training at sampling rate 0.5 is only 32% faster than SAM.
record.recipe_differences: Introduces an asymptotically unbiased, dynamic sample-selection method for SAM based on estimated average gradient norms; evaluates it against SAM and SGD.
record.method_sensitivity: The sampling rate α changes the reported accuracy and speed; effects also differ by architecture and dataset. The authors state that smaller networks can be more affected by omitting low-gradient samples.

fits_no_version.finding: AUSAM trades sampling rate against training speed and accuracy. At sampling rate 0.5, CIFAR accuracy is numerically below SAM in all recorded comparisons; Tiny-ImageNet differences vary by architecture. Reported speed ratios also vary substantially.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-based dynamic sample selection can accelerate SAM while retaining approximately similar held-out accuracy in some image-classification settings.

fits_no_version.finding: AUSAM reports a pose mean score of 89.5 versus SAM's 89.4, and QAT accuracies of 89.63 versus 89.75 for ResNet-18 and 84.91 versus 84.72 for MobileNetV1, with faster training than SAM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AUSAM can accelerate SAM in pose estimation and quantization-aware training while retaining similar task performance.

record.problems: No training error or train-test gap is reported, so the tables cannot establish changes in the gap. Main accuracy experiments use three random seeds and report standard deviations. Some comparison-method results in Table 2 are explicitly reported from prior work.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 contains additional comparison methods and AUSAM sampling rates. These were omitted to stay within the row limit after retaining SAM, SGD, and AUSAM-0.5 or AUSAM-0.4 comparisons for each listed CIFAR model and dataset; reported-from-prior-work methods were excluded as non-study results. Tiny-ImageNet AUSAM-0.6 rows were omitted because the table's AUSAM-0.5 rows cover the stated comparable-accuracy condition. Table 5's data-pruning comparisons were omitted because they compare methods, not the study's sample-selection result. Table 1's α parameter-study values duplicate the CIFAR-100 rows retained from Table 2.

untested.parts: No fixed random-label fitting or comparison of natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
No width sweep beyond the width required for zero training error.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison or test of learned local connectivity.
No adaptive-optimizer-versus-SGD comparison on the same workload under specified tuning budgets.
No controlled large-batch sweep or workload-dependent threshold. AUSAM changes sample selection together with effective batch size and retains the original iteration count.
No dropout ablation or joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
No magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, measured generalization gaps, or comparison of sharpness rankings with norm and margin measures.
No influence-based memorization scores or removal of highly memorized examples followed by retraining against equal-sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: None of the listed versions receives a verdict. The exclusion rests on mismatched experimental questions, not merely missing training-error measurements: held-out accuracy would suffice for several versions if the required comparisons were present. Gradient norms used for dynamic sampling are not V8's memorization scores, and SAM's perturbation objective is not V7's magnitude-aware generalization measure.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization under tuning choices.
Large batches and fixed-epoch generalization gap.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a predictor of generalization gap.
